_schema._comment: CANONICAL SOURCE of state Medigap (Medicare Supplement) regulatory data for the planned Medicare (Medigap vs. Medicare Advantage) tool. Deliberately a SEPARATE file from roth-conversion/states.json — that file's own _schema documents it as the canonical source of state TAX data specifically; Medigap rating and switching-rights rules are insurance regulation, a different domain, and mixing them would blur the single-purpose boundary each canonical file is supposed to have (see README.md's 'note on the engine boundary'). All data here traces back to _dev/medicare-research-2026-08.md, the research working doc this file was built from — consult it for the full reasoning, corrections made mid-research, and what's still unverified.
_schema.scopeDecision: This tool does NOT assert a dollar premium for any state — there is no primary source for actual Medigap premiums (insurer-set, vary by company/age/state, no IRS-Rev-Proc equivalent exists). The user supplies their own real quoted premium, same pattern as Roth's retRate field. This file's job is to correctly model the STATE RULES that shape how that premium behaves over time and what switching rights exist, not to guess the premium itself.

confidenceLevels.PRIMARY: Read the actual statute/regulation text or an official government page directly.
confidenceLevels.OFFICIAL-SUMMARY: Confirmed via an official government page/press release, but the underlying statute text itself wasn't read directly.
confidenceLevels.SECONDARY-CORROBORATED: Confirmed only via summaries of secondary sources (law firm blogs, insurance broker sites, aggregators), but a specific citation was named and multiple independent sources agree.
confidenceLevels.UNVERIFIED: Sources disagree or no citation was found. Present in the schema as a real gap, not silently omitted — do not treat as fact.

fields.benefitStructure: "standard" for the 47 states using the federal A-N lettered plan system, or "custom" for Massachusetts, Minnesota, and Wisconsin, which standardize Medigap differently. Custom states have a customPlanNote pointing to the plain-language description in the research doc rather than a full re-encoded benefit grid — that grid is reference/educational content, not something the breakeven computation needs to consume, so it's deliberately not modeled field-by-field here.
fields.rating.method: One of: "community" (premium never varies by age within your Medicare-eligibility category — see rating.disabilitySplit), "issueAgeMandated" (insurer MUST price by enrollment age, cannot use attained-age — currently unused; Florida was previously classified here but downgraded 2026-08-20 when the claimed citation didn't hold up under direct primary-source checking, see FL's own note), "attainedAgeBanned" (attained-age specifically prohibited, but issuer may choose issue-age OR community — Arizona, Georgia), "noMandate" (no state law restricts the method; attained-age is the prevailing market default but this is insurer choice, not a guarantee), or "unverified" (Missouri, Florida — sources conflict or don't support a specific claim; do not encode a specific method).
fields.rating.disabilitySplit: Boolean. true means the state's community-rating law explicitly permits a SEPARATE community rate for people who qualify for Medicare by disability rather than by age (Idaho, Vermont, Washington). The accurate description of these states' rule is 'premium doesn't vary by age within your eligibility category', not a flat 'never varies by age' — do not drop this qualifier when surfacing the fact to a user.
fields.guaranteedIssuePeriods: Array, can hold zero or more entries — most states have zero (federal one-time 6-month window only). Each entry describes ONE distinct annual/ongoing right to switch or newly enroll in a Medigap plan without medical underwriting, beyond the federal baseline. Deliberately an array of typed objects (not fixed fields for 'birthday rule' specifically) so a new guaranteed-issue trigger type can be added without a schema change — validated twice: once for West Virginia's lossOfMedicaidEligibility, and again for the employerRetireeCoverageChange trigger (28 states, see research doc section 12).
fields.guaranteedIssuePeriods[].trigger: "birthday" | "policyAnniversary" (Missouri — the POLICY's anniversary date, not the person's birthday) | "annualEnrollmentPeriod" (tied to a federal Medicare enrollment calendar, but the exact window varies by state — Rhode Island is just the Oct15-Dec7 AEP; Minnesota is broader, combining the AEP with the Jan1-Mar31 MA Open Enrollment Period per 42 CFR 422.62(a)(2)-(4) — always check windowAnchor for the state-specific shape rather than assuming the trigger name alone tells you the dates) | "insurerChosenWindow" (Maine — a fixed annual window whose TIMING the insurer picks, not anchored to the person's birthday, the policy date, or a state-set calendar) | "continuous" (no window at all — right exists year-round) | "lossOfMedicaidEligibility" (West Virginia — a specific life-event trigger, not a calendar window; found by reading a state's full primary-source bill text rather than secondary summaries, which is exactly the kind of thing this schema's extensible trigger-type design (rather than fixed fields) exists to accommodate without a restructure) | "employerRetireeCoverageChange" (28 states — a life-event trigger fired when an employer changes, but doesn't eliminate, a Medicare beneficiary's retiree health coverage; broader than the federal baseline, which only covers full elimination. Sourced to KFF's Yes/No state list, not per-state statute text — see windowDays/insurerScope/benefitLevel below for what's deliberately left unverified on these entries.).
fields.guaranteedIssuePeriods[].appliesTo: "existingHoldersOnly" (must already hold a Medigap policy — true for Washington, Missouri, and all the birthday-rule states) vs "anyone" (the right extends to people who never had Medigap before — confirmed for New York, Connecticut, and Massachusetts). This distinction was wrong in an earlier draft of this file (NY/CT/MA were incorrectly narrowed to existingHoldersOnly, matching Washington) — caught and fixed during the adversarial pass, see git history.
fields.guaranteedIssuePeriods[].windowDays: Integer, or null. null means either trigger:"continuous" (no window applies), OR the window length genuinely isn't known — the source only confirmed the right exists, not its exact parameters (all 28 employerRetireeCoverageChange entries; distinguish the two null cases via the confidence/note fields, not this field alone).
fields.guaranteedIssuePeriods[].windowAnchor: Free-text description of when the window starts relative to the trigger, e.g. "30 days before, 30+ after" or "1st of birthday month" — deliberately not further structured since the shapes genuinely vary per state (see research doc section 5) and forcing them into rigid start/end offset fields lost real precision when drafted that way. null when not independently known (see windowDays).
fields.guaranteedIssuePeriods[].insurerScope: "any" | "sameInsurer" | "sameOrAffiliatedInsurer" | null (not independently verified — do not assume "any" as a default; the 28 employerRetireeCoverageChange entries deliberately leave this null rather than guess).
fields.guaranteedIssuePeriods[].benefitLevel: "equalOrLesser" (the near-universal restriction, applies to switching-type rights where there's a prior policy to compare against — birthday rules, Missouri's anniversary rule) | "any" (Rhode Island, New York, Connecticut, Massachusetts — confirmed more generous; note this is also the structurally correct value for any continuous/anyone right, since 'equal or lesser than PRIOR coverage' is a concept that doesn't apply to someone with no prior Medigap policy at all) | null (not independently verified — same employerRetireeCoverageChange caveat as insurerScope).
fields.guaranteedIssuePeriods[].restrictions: Free-text: age caps, prior-coverage requirements, or other conditions that don't fit the structured fields above (e.g. Illinois' ages-65-to-75 cap, West Virginia's 24-month continuous-prior-coverage requirement).
fields.guaranteedIssuePeriods[].effectiveDate: ISO date. May be in the future (New Mexico: 2027-01-01) — check against today's date before treating as live; see notYetEffective.
fields.guaranteedIssuePeriods[].notYetEffective: Boolean, present and true only for laws enacted but not yet in force as of this file's last update. Same pattern as Roth's Oklahoma bracket handling: use the state's prior/baseline status until the effective date passes, and disclose the pending change.
fields.citation: Legal citation (statute/regulation number) where found, or a plain description of the source (official agency page, press release) when no statute number was pinned down.
fields.confidence: One of the four confidenceLevels above.
fields.lastVerified: ISO date this specific fact was last checked against a source. Recheck triggers in the research doc (Delaware effective-date ambiguity, West Virginia and New Mexico's effective dates, Rhode Island's very-new law) should be re-verified before this file backs a live, shipped tool.

guaranteedIssuePeriods.restrictions: ages 65-75 only. The statute separately guarantees under-65 disabled Medicare enrollees issue in several situations (fully losing employer coverage, an Advantage plan leaving their area, insurer insolvency) and bars charging them more than the highest 65+ rate for the same plan (215 ILCS 5/363(6),(10)) — a distinct, under-65 disability-linked category, not modeled here. guaranteedIssuePeriods.note: Read directly from the statute text (ilga.gov, 2026-08-20), upgraded from SECONDARY-CORROBORATED. guaranteedIssuePeriods.restrictions: Must apply to an insurer DIFFERENT from the one that issued the applicant's current Medigap policy — a mandatory different-issuer requirement, the same unusual shape found in Indiana (not merely 'any' insurer being allowed). Also narrower than the standard equalOrLesser pattern: the applicant must seek to maintain the SAME Medicare supplement plan letter, not merely an equal-or-lesser one. R. & Regs. 0780-01-58-.15 'Guaranteed Issue for Eligible Persons'): 'The individual is enrolled under Title XIX of the Social Security Act (Medicaid) and the enrollment involuntarily ceases after the individual is sixty-five (65) years of age or older and eligible for and enrolled in Medicare Part B.' Distinguished from the separate, universal federal suspend/reinstate-while-on-Medicaid mechanism (present in nearly every state's minimum-standards regulation, e.g. Hawaii's and Utah's) — this is a genuinely distinct new-purchase right, matching what KFF's Table 3 column measures.

Code R590-146-12, not yet read directly) — left unencoded rather than guessed, consistent with this file's no-unsourced-numbers rule.

guaranteedIssuePeriods.note: Read directly from the codified statute text (le.utah.gov, 2026-08-20) — confirmed exactly: 'Each year, beginning on an enrollee's birthday and ending 60 days later, an issuer shall allow an enrollee that is enrolled in one of the issuer's Medicare supplement insurance plans to choose a different Medicare supplement insurance plan that is (A) offered by the issuer; and (B) considered a comparable or lower tier plan than the enrollee's current plan. An issuer may not deny enrollment based on medical underwriting...'

guaranteedIssuePeriods.windowAnchor: starts on birthday, guaranteed open at least 60 days (insurer may extend)
guaranteedIssuePeriods.restrictions: Narrower than the standard equalOrLesser pattern: the new policy must offer the SAME benefits as current coverage, not merely equal-or-lesser (e.g. Plan G to Plan G only) — same shape as Kentucky's same-plan-only requirement. 'Innovative benefits' (vision, hearing, dental riders) are excluded when comparing benefit levels. If the policyholder bought their Medigap policy in Virginia but has since moved out of state, they still receive the required notice, but any policy they switch to during the window is governed by the laws of their new state of residence, not Virginia's. Insurer must send written notice 15-30 days before the enrollee's birthday, disclosing the window dates, rights, and any benefit/premium changes to the current policy.
guaranteedIssuePeriods.citation: Va. Code § 38.2-3611, enacted by 2025 Va. Acts chs. 530, 540 (HB 2100)
guaranteedIssuePeriods.note: Found 2026-08-20 via a birthday-rule cross-check against multiple secondary sources naming Virginia as a recent (2024-2026) enactor — this state's entry previously had only the generic KFF employer-retiree-coverage-change line, missing this real, significant right entirely. Confirmed directly against the codified statute text (law.lis.virginia.gov) and the Virginia Bureau of Insurance's own consumer guide, both agreeing precisely: 'annual open enrollment period commencing on the day of the individual's birthday and remaining open for at least 60 days thereafter,' 'any insurer in the Commonwealth,' and 'the same benefits as those provided by the current coverage.'

rating.note: Up to two rating pools (age- vs. disability-eligible); spousal-discount and payment-method variation also allowed. Read directly (2026-08-20), upgraded from SECONDARY-CORROBORATED — confirmed word-for-word: 'may vary premiums based on spousal discounts, frequency of payment, and method of payment... and may develop no more than two rating pools that distinguish between an insured's eligibility for medicare by reason of: (a) Age; or (b) Disability.'

guaranteedIssuePeriods.restrictions: Existing holders replacing one Medigap policy with another, restricted to switching within the same plan group (Plan A only replaceable by another Plan A; any of plans B/C/D/E/F/G/K/L by another in that same broader group) — confirmed directly. The commonly-repeated '90+ days of prior coverage' figure was NOT found in this section, nor in the related guaranteed-issue statute (§ 48.66.055, entirely federal-baseline-style categories unrelated to this right) or the application-form regulation (WAC 284-66-130) — checked all three directly and none contain it. Left as an unconfirmed, likely broker-sourced detail rather than reasserted as fact; the core switching right itself is confirmed.
guaranteedIssuePeriods.note: Read directly (2026-08-20), upgraded from SECONDARY-CORROBORATED. Corrected citation from § 48.66.055 (Washington's codification of the standard federal-baseline guaranteed-issue categories — employer coverage loss, Advantage plan termination, trial rights — nothing about this switching right) to § 48.66.045(1)-(2), the actual source: issuers must accept a replacement Medigap application without medical underwriting, with plans B-L getting broader within-group portability than Plan A (only replaceable by another Plan A).

guaranteedIssuePeriods.restrictions: requires 24 MONTHS of continuous prior coverage under the same or an affiliated insurer, without a lapse; each replacement policy resets the 24-month clock before it can be replaced again — the most restrictive prior-coverage requirement found in this research. Exception: if neither the insurer nor its affiliates have accepted new applications for that plan type in the past 12 months, the right extends to any authorized insurer instead. The 60-day window is an APPLICATION window only — the new policy's effective date doesn't have to fall within it, and can be delayed up to 90 days at the applicant's request to coordinate with the old policy's termination.
guaranteedIssuePeriods.citation: W. Va. Code § 33-15F-1(b) (HB 4869, 2026 Reg. Sess.)
guaranteedIssuePeriods.note: Read directly from the enrolled bill text (2026-08-20), upgraded from SECONDARY-CORROBORATED. The bill's own cover page cites a general 'in effect 90 days from passage (June 11, 2026)' date, but the substantive applicability clause, subsection (g), specifically ties this right to policies delivered/issued/reissued/extended on or after June 1, 2026 — used the more specific, operative figure. The bill text explicitly excludes Medicare Advantage plans (subsection (f)(4)).

guaranteedIssuePeriods.windowAnchor: starts the date Medicaid eligibility ends
guaranteedIssuePeriods.restrictions: must be 65+, entitled to Medicare, and losing Title XIX (Medicaid) eligibility, including full or partial dual eligibility. Applies regardless of whether previously enrolled in a Medigap policy, and regardless of whether the person was Medicaid-eligible when first entitled to Medicare. Does NOT apply solely because of disenrolling from a Medicare Advantage plan.
guaranteedIssuePeriods.citation: W. Va. Code § 33-15F-1(c) (HB 4869, 2026 Reg. Sess.)
guaranteedIssuePeriods.note: A second, entirely separate guaranteed-issue right under the same bill — missed by every secondary source found during the original research pass, caught only by reading the full enrolled bill text directly. WI.customPlanNote: Not multiple lettered plans at all — ONE base plan (Part A coinsurance for hospital/SNF/hospice, 175 lifetime days of extra inpatient mental health care, 40 extra home health visits, Part B 20% coinsurance, 3 pints of blood/year, state-mandated benefits) with OPTIONAL add-on riders (Part A deductible, more home health visits, Part B deductible, Part B excess charge, foreign travel, a partial Part A deductible option, Part B copay/coinsurance). Separate '50%/25% Cost-Sharing Plans' resemble K/L; a high-deductible variant also exists. Full detail in _dev/medicare-research-2026-08.md section 2.

guaranteedIssuePeriods.note: Multiple independent, consistent sources describe this exact shape (63 days from birthday, eff. Jun 4, 2025). Code R. § 35-12 ('Guaranteed Issue for Eligible Persons'), read directly, is Wyoming's codification of the standard federal-baseline categories (employer coverage loss, Advantage plan termination, trial rights) — structurally identical to Washington's § 48.66.055 and Minnesota's Subd. 1u, nothing about a birthday rule.
